pending_news.title: Tony Iommi on writing metal’s greatest riff: “You never know when the magic’s going to strike”
pending_news.rss_body:
As his new solo album

From The Dark

proves,

Tony Iommi

remains the king of the riff. The Dark Lord laid won the blueprint for an entire genre with the immortal riff that opens

Black Sabbath

’s eponymous 1970 debut album, an he’s not stopped since.

When

Metal Hammer

conducted a poll in 2018 to find the greatest riff of all time, it was no surprise that he was behind the one that came out on top. To be fair, any number of Sabbath riffs could have stolen it –

Iron Man

,

Sweet Leaf

,

Hole In The Sky

,

Paranoid

,

Black Sabbath

itself… the list goes on.

But the actual winner? The monumental riff that powers

Symptom Of The Universe

, the classic track from Sabbath’s 1975 album

Sabotage

. We asked the man behind how he created this immortal noise.

Can you remember where you were when you came up with the riff for

Symptom Of The Universe

?

Tony Iommi: “Oh my god, it was a long time ago. I can’t remember, to be completely truthful. I imagine we would have probably been in rehearsal.”

Is that how you used to come up with riffs – in rehearsal?

“Generally, yeah. Sometimes I’ve come up with stuff at home and taped it just to remember it, but I don’t really work things out as such.”

You make it sound easy…

“Dare I say it, but yeah, I’ve not had much trouble coming up with riffs. Now I’ve said it, I’ll probably never come up with another one. But I’ve got hundreds of them from over the years on various CDs. Some of them go back to the original

Sabbath

, some from the

Dio

era, bits and bobs from when [Deep Purple’s] Ian Gillan or [former vocalist] Tony Martin were in the band. I don’t even know what’s on there. I keep threatening to sit down and listen to them all one of these days when I get the chance.”

(Image credit: Gus Stewart/Redferns)

Back when you were writing

Symptom Of The Universe

, which guitarists were you in competition with?

“Me. I was in competition with myself. I would always try to come up with more and more inventive ideas – different tunings, changing the amps, just fiddling about with the guitars really. I would constantly be trying to improve things and change things. I didn’t really listen to other people, just in case I started playing someone else’s riff by mistake.”

The second half of

Symptom Of The Universe

heads off into weird, prog-jazz territory. Was that you deliberately setting out to write an early prog metal song?

“No, that was just us jamming together. It was something I came up with and Geezer [Butler, bass] and Bill [Ward, drums] followed, and then Ozzy came in. But then a lot of Sabbath’s stuff went to places you didn’t think they would go. I remember when we had Ronnie Dio with us, I played him the track

Die Young

[which ended up on Sabbath’s

Heaven And Hell

album]. It went into this completely different tempo, and he went, ‘You can’t do that!’ I went, ‘Of course we can. It’s what we’ve always done.’”

What are your memories of making Sympton Of The Universe’s parent album,

Sabotage

?

“Oh, it was a nightmare. We had a court case with our ex-manager, Patrick Meehan, while we were in the middle of making the album. We’d get a writ and we’d end up having to go into bloody court in the morning, all dressed up, then try to get back to the studio afterwards to carry on working. It was hard to come up with things. You had to have two heads.”

Did that aggro feed into the album?

“Certainly with Geezer’s lyrics. He wrote one song called

The Writ

, so it influenced him, that’s for sure. I think the aggression definitely came out in the music when we played together. There is some really heavy stuff on that record.”

Is it true that

The Writ

was inspired by a lawyer unexpectedly turning up at the studio to serve you with legal papers?

“That’s exactly what happened. They used to turn up all the bloody time. We never knew they were coming. If we did, we’d have disappeared sharpish.”

Sabotage

took nearly a year to record. Was there ever a point where you thought you might not make it to the end?

“No, I’ve never felt like that. We’ve always fought through whatever was there. Without the music, we’d have all gone bloody loony. I think it actually it brought us all together as a band. Whenever we went through problems, we’d just fight through it together.”

(Image credit: Kevin Mazur/WireImage)

The

Sabotage

album cover. What’s going on there?

“Ha ha ha! A guy who worked for us who was an artist, he came up with a great idea – us reflected in a mirror, stuff like that. But when it got to the day, somebody said to Bill, ‘What are you gonna wear?’ And he was, like, ‘I dunno.’ So he turned to his wife and said, ‘Can I borrow your tights?’ So he put on this pair of his wife’s red tights. And I think he might have borrowed Ozzy’s underpants, too. It looked bloody ridiculous. It definitely didn’t come out like we wanted it to.”

When was the last time you came up with a riff and thought, ‘Ooh, that’s a bit tasty’?

“Well, I’ve got a few that I haven’t used yet that were good. There’s about four or five from the last Sabbath album [

13

] I that we didn’t use. I listened to a CD with them on recently. I thought, ‘Blimey, that’s good, why didn’t we use it?’”

We’ve talked about Symptom Of The Universe. But what’s your favourite Tony Iommi riff?

“Oh my god, that’s difficult. I like

Into The Void

. And I like some of the stuff we did with Dio –

Heaven And Hell

was a good riff,

Neon Knights

. There’s so many I like. I like pretty much all the stuff we’ve done.”

Apart from your own, what’s the greatest riff of all time?

“That’s even harder. There’s so many great riffs out there from the past, and up to date stuff. But you’ve got to have Deep Purple’s

Smoke On The Water

. And of course there are a lot of Zeppelin songs. Jimmy Page has some great riffs.”

Have you ever had a riff come into your head while you’ve been sitting on the toilet?

“Ha ha! Oh yeah. I have riffs that come in all the time at different times, different places. You never know when the magic’s going to strike.”

This interview originally appeared in Metal Hammer issue 311

pending_news.rss_body:
Shaun the Sheep's latest foray into Hollywood might have been significantly more metal if

Black Sabbath

guitarist

Tony Iommi

had agreed to write the theme music.

Iommi has revealed he was approached to contribute to the score for this year's movie

Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom

, but had to turn it down because he was too busy.

The in-demand musician was working on

a track with Robbie Williams

when the request came in last year. And he was also getting ready to work with William Shatner on

his heavy metal project

, as well as his own new solo album

From The Dark

.

With all of that to contend with, Iommi simply didn't have the capacity to get involved in the hugely successful animation franchise.

Asked about the most "bizarre thing" he had ever worked on in his career, Iommi tells Planet Rock: "Apart from Sabbath you mean? I was asked to do Shaun the Sheep as well. I didn't do that!

"They were doing a movie and they wanted some theme music for it. But no, we'd got too much on. I'd done the Robbie thing and trying to do my own album, then the William Shatner thing. That's enough for now!"

Iommi joked that he wouldn't rule out taking on a project like Shaun the Sheep in the future, adding that "it'll be Peppa Pig next."

He also discussed Sabbath's 1983 album

Born Again

with Ian GIllan on vocals. Widely considered the band's most controversial album, fans – and Gillan himself – have spoken about the quality of the record's production.

Iommi says he does plan to have the album remixed.

He says: "Yes, there is a plan. To be honest, we couldn't find those tapes for a long time. They disappeared.

"But they were in some record company storage. And anyway, we've gotten them back and they were transferred. So they are ready to start work on."

pending_news.title: AI Ozzy won't be "selling cell phones" insists Jack Osbourne
pending_news.rss_body:
Jack Osbourne says he shoulders the blame for

the backlash to controversial plans

to produce an AI version of his late father

Ozzy

.

When the digital Ozzy was announced, Jack said his father "would be into" it.

He and his mother Sharon later stressed

that it was not the ghoulish cash grab that some fans had branded it, saying instead that it was about ensuring the

Black Sabbath

icon would be remembered.

Now in a new interview for Great Company With Jamie Laing, Jack insists the digital version of his dad won't be used for anything tacky like selling cell phones and admits his naivety was to blame for the backlash.

Jack, 40, says: "The backlash, it was my own fault. We'd just kind of figured this thing out, that we were gonna do it, and I guess I wasn't properly armed with the way to properly explain what it was.

"And I think people thought that next thing it's gonna be Ozzy Osbourne selling cell phones. No."

He adds that they family wanted get out in front of the rapidly growing artificial intelligence landscape by making sure they retained the rights to Ozzy's digital IP (intellectual property).

"A lot of people are doing this now," he says. "Creating the AI model and creating the digital fingerprint of whoever – whether it's my father or Bob Marley's people are doing it, and Michael Jackson's team are doing it.

"By kind of creating this digital fingerprint, you ultimately will own the digital IP and image of that person. And so as to what it can be used for now, yeah, there's a handful of things.

"But down the road, it's where things are going. It's no different than saying, 'I wanna own my images of my father. I wanna own his intellectual property,'

"It's just another avenue. And the fact that AI is what it is, it's not going anywhere, it's not changing. It was our choice to go, 'Hey, we should be out in front of this, and we should not be on the back foot with having this kind of new pillar of entertainment properly locked down.'"

The digital Ozzy plan sees the family teaming up with Hyperreal for the project they are calling

The Enduring Legacy of a Rock Icon and His Family: Ozzy Osbourne and The Osbournes.

The Cult: Sonic Temple

(Image credit: Beggars Banquet)

Sun King

Fire Woman

American Horse

Edie (Ciao Baby)

Sweet Soul Sister

Soul Asylum

New York City

Automatic Blues

Soldier Blue

Wake Up Time for Freedom

Sonic Temple

was

The Cult

in their pomp, their ultimate bid to become the biggest band on the planet. They didn’t manage it, but they did leave behind this glorious monument to lyrical hubris and sonic excess.

Produced by Bob Rock, their fourth album took their usual preoccupations – glamorous losers on

Edie (Ciao Baby)

, the suffering of indigenes on

American Horse

– and turned up the noise.

Soul Asylum

was pure Zep worship,

Fire Woman

their wailing, throbbing apotheosis, while

Sun King

seemed to acknowledge that The Cult knew they’d reached their limit (‘

This is where it all ends

’).

"It was a little careerist, for sure," guitarist

Billy Duffy

told us. "I don’t think Ian [Astbury, frontman] resisted that, but I don’t think he viewed it from the same perspective, either. I think he saw it as being more psychedelic.

"I think he saw it as having more of

Cream

,

Disraeli Gears

sorta vibe, more than my sort of ultimate schoolboy rock album idea. You know, no-holds-barred, punk is finally over; I just want to have a full-fledged rock album while I’m at the prime of my powers kinda thing. So maybe I took the lead on this one."

Stream on Spotify

Stream on Apple Music

Every week, Album of the Week Club listens to and discusses the album in question, votes on how good it is, and publishes our findings, with the aim of giving people reliable reviews and the wider rock community the chance to contribute.

Join the group now

.

Best Wishes - Cro-Mags

Repeat Offender - Richard Marx

Mr. Music Head - Adrian Belew

1,000 Hours - Green Day

The Black Swan - The Triffids

The Headless Children - W.A.S.P.

Slippery When Ill - The Vandals

What they said...

"

Sonic Temple

finds the Cult trying several different metal styles, from crunchy Electric-era '70s grooves and the fuzzy, noisy psychedelia of Love, to mellow ballads and commercial '80s hard rock. Not all of the experiments work, as some of the songs lean toward ponderousness, but enough of them do to send

Sonic Temple

into the Billboard Top Ten, due to the exposure provided by the hit single

Fire Woman

." (

AllMusic

)

"This is the past recycled. Which is quite different from revamping it. It's the definitive Cult LP, Astbury tells us, and

Sonic Temple

, what with its supposed references to their drippy spirituality and granite hard rockisms, is the definitive title.

Soul Asylum

is Astbury at prayer, at one with his 'precious child', the 'sweet warm goddess', proving himself the only rocker brave enough to admit to not pulling the wings off little insects." (

Record Mirror

)

"Though they’ve run a bit short on good riffs this time, it’s possible to put

Sonic Temple

on and have a perfectly fine time with the big beat (this was cut with studio drummer Mickey Currey before new drummer Matt Sorum joined), big guitar noise and Ian Astbury’s ragged, not-too-high-pitched vocal histrionics, if you don’t think too hard. But

sheesh

, is it stupid." (

Los Angeles Times

)

What you said...

Nick Tedds:

Following the psychedelic/goth infused

Love

and the raw, hardened edginess of

Electric

came the third in the trilogy of what I consider to be The Cult's best work.

Sonic Temple

blends some of the finest elements from the previous two albums, mixed with a dollop of Bob Rock-crafted sheen, leading to one of the stronger rock albums from the late eighties.

The opening tracks,

Sun King

and

Fire Woman,

set the tone and a very high bar indeed; all big riffs, played at a blistering pace. When affairs settle down a little, mid-tempo, atmospheric, bluesy numbers such as

Soul Asylum

offer balance but no let-up in terms of quality. I admit that

Edie (Ciao Baby)

was a little bit of a slow burner for me at the time of release, but I now appreciate the full glory of this emotional ballad, whilst the catchy

Soldier Blue

gallops along to a pounding beat as matters begin to draw to a close.

Billy Duffy is on fire throughout, revelling in the freedom offered by songs that often hit home instantaneously and have, for the most part, stood the test of time. There are also not many vocalists that can match Ian Astbury on his day, in terms of range, swagger and all-round wailing ability.

Brett E Wells

: This album was released during the final weeks of my senior year of college. It was responsible for the destruction of the woofers in my dorm room speakers. All these years later, I still play it loud.

Chris Downie

: Few bands in the classic rock era were more aptly monikered than The Cult, being as they were one of the biggest and best cult bands of the era, one that reinvented itself multiple times, to often enthralling effect. From their psychedelic goth-punk roots as Southern Death Cult, to the AC/DC, Cream and Rolling Stones worship of 1987's

Electric

and the indie-rock-inflected self-titled 1994 effort, they never stood still and remained as hard to pigeonhole as they were to predict.

For many fans, however, their peak is usually argued as a toss-up between the gothic alt-rock of 1985's

Love

and 1989's arena rock masterpiece

Sonic Temple

. While the former had the smash hits of

Rain

and

She Sells Sanctuary

and brilliant deeper cuts like

Hollow Man

, the latter saw them shamelessly rock out in a manner that perhaps should have seen them reach even greater commercial heights; from the MTV hits like

Fire Woman

to the mini-epic of

Soul Asylum

(arguably a nod to Zeppelin's

Kashmir

), there is barely a weak moment to be found here.

It could be argued their eclecticism, while undoubtedly one of their strong points - if not the strongest - was also their biggest drawback, in that their refusal to stand still and choose a lane, as it were, saw fans of many subgenres come and go over the years.

Sonic Temple

remains perhaps their most accessible, mainstream offering, but one they struggled to live down since; 1991's

Ceremony

was a spirited follow-up and the aforementioned 1994 eponymous release an experimental stab at modernisation, while the metallic sounds of their 2001 comeback saw a renaissance that continues on and off to this day, but they never again sounded this huge.

Bob Rock deserves huge credit for bringing out the arena rock in them, and if there's only one criticism to be had, it's in the way it tails off in quality over the last three tracks. Had

Wake Up Time

been dropped to B-side status and the 11 tracks trimmed to 10, you would have a practically flawless classic. In any case, this is one of at least three albums in their canon that stand the test of time and affirm their brilliance. 9/10.

Brian Carr

: My preteen and teenage years were mostly in the 80s, so MTV was a tremendously important part of my musical education. I still have tremendous fondness for that era, but in hindsight I can also see how the visual could be a detriment to budding young musical minds. The Cult were on my periphery with the albums

Electric

and

Sonic Temple

, but I have a suspicion that something about their image struck me as a little weird, at least compared to my favourite bands of the time. Or maybe I just didn’t dig Ian Astbury’s voice. Whatever the reason, while I didn’t hate the tunes that I heard from those two records, there wasn’t enough at the time to make me want to listen deeper.

Which turns out to be a shame, because

Sonic Temple

is a damned fine rock record. First and foremost, Billy Duffy’s guitar playing is fantastic on this record. I know The Cult went through different musical sounds/stages in their career, and Duffy probably didn’t always play as he does here, but this is definitely in my wheelhouse, and certainly justifies the cover artwork. As for Astbury’s voice, it’s interesting - his vocal delivery reminds me of Andrew Wood from Mother Love Bone, not in tone, but in his phrasing. And I loved Mother Love Bone. And it turns out that grown-up me is just fine with his voice.

So with this week’s Album choice, I’m going from two rarely listened-to songs in my Apple Music library to the entire record being added, with the likelihood of more attention on my part. And it only took 37 years for me to get there!

Greg Schwepe

: So, readers, raise your right hand (as Billy Duffy is doing) if the first time you saw the cover of

Sonic Temple

you immediately said to yourself (or out loud!) “Hell yeah! I bet this album f***ing

rocks!

” Right? This is a case where you

can

judge an album by its cover, and you get it 100% right. There’s Billy, feet splayed, arm raised high to windmill a power chord on his Les Paul Custom. Just like Pete Townshend. And the same pose that Jack Black instructed his young guitarist protege to make in

School Of Rock.

When you make a statement like that on the cover, you better deliver, correct? And The Cult totally delivered on

Sonic Temple

. Almost an hour of crunching riffs that keep coming. There’s no letup, and not one song I don’t like. As I listened multiple times again today, it was a steady stream of “damn, that one’s good too” as I went through the tracks. And I found this happening at the tail end of the album, where a lot of times a band seems to lose its steam. I might venture that the second half of the album is stronger than the first half. But then again, the first half is pretty damn good too!

My first encounter with The Cult was via MTV, and not radio. And I will admit, they kinda confused me. They were kind of a contradiction in styles. Watching the video for

Fire Woman

, you had this kick-ass mainstream rock song. But you had a wall of amps in the performance video that screamed metal, but the hairstyles screamed goth or punk. And the bell bottoms Ian Astbury was wearing kind of said 70s hippie. I sure as heck couldn’t pigeonhole this band, but I sure as heck liked them. FM radio around me was slow to embrace them because they couldn’t be put in a specific box. But once you get a kick-ass track like

Fire Woman

, that finally fit in nicely with the normal Midwest FM radio AC/DC/Zeppelin/Aerosmith/ZZ Top rotation they were playing.

This is my go-to Cult album (with

Electric

being a close second). Again, the tracks are just relentless, and the energy never lets up. 8 out of 10 on this one for me. Buy it for the cover vibe, stay for the music that backs it up.

Philip Qvist

: A friend of mine gave me the best description of The Cult during their 80s peak by stating that they acted as though they were behind and ahead of the rock music curve, both at the same time. This confused both the casual listener and record companies. I mean, how do you pigeonhole a band that refuses to listen to the rules? In addition, they never seemed to hold onto a drummer for more than six months.

Despite all that, though, in the space of four years they released three absolute classics:

Love

in 1985, the superb

Electric

in 1987 and arguably their peak with

Sonic Temple

in 1989. And this neatly brings us to this week's review.

The album includes three iconic singles:

Fire Woman, Sweet Soul Sister

and

Edie (Ciao Baby)

, their tribute to the ill-fated Edie Sedgwick and easily my favourite ever song from The Cult. But it is the other tracks such as

Sun King, American Horse

, the epic

Soul Asylum

and

Soldier Blue

that always bring me back to Sonic Temple. Yes, it does run out of a bit of steam after

Soul Asylum

, but that is relative, as many bands would have loved to have had a

New York City

or

Automatic Blues

on their record.

You can argue over which is the band's best album, and

Electric

definitely runs it close, but for me

Sonic Temple

was their peak. Bassist Jamie Stewart would depart from the band a year later, while the relationship between the band's songwriters, mainly singer Ian Astbury and (the underrated) guitarist Billy Duffy, would begin to sour, with a corresponding drop in quality on later albums (they were still good though).

Sonic Temple

rocks and it has great songs on it. It is my favourite Cult album for a reason. 9/10 from me.

Mark Herrington

: Undeniably,

Sonic Temple

is a very good rock album, but the Cult had lost something by this point. I had started out listening to Southern Death Cult, then Death Cult and those initial albums of the Cult, which still retained much of that mystical strangeness that typified them.

It's probably why I prefer

Fire Woman

and

Sweet Soul Sister

most here, as they retain a flavour of that earlier stuff. The rest here is very good, but lacks much of their unique Goth character. For that, I would always choose

Love

over this.

Craig Glenn:

Not a bad album, but I think they nailed it on the previous album,

Electric,

which was full-on rock. They should have stuck with Rick Rubin instead of switching to Bob Rock as producer. They got back on that Indian spiritual stuff with this, then went full-blown with it on

Ceremony,

which is far from their best.

Paul Cropper

: After trying to be AC/DC on

Electric

(another great album), The Cult turn into a bombastic American arena rock group. Love it.

Mike Chronakis

: By far their greatest album for me. So many great songs on there, especially

Fire Woman

and

Sun King

.

Mike Ginsberg

: An incredible album following another incredible album, both of which are underrated classics.

Joe Cogan

: Their best album, with the epic

Soul Asylum

as their artistic pinnacle.

Adam Ranger

: As a callow youth, I saw this band when they were supporting Sisters of Mercy. They were Southern Death Cult back then, of course. At the time I liked goth, and I liked rock, but I have to say I was a bit dismissive when they became the Cult and went full rock band.

However, as I have aged, I have (generally) become less dismissive of such things and have learnt to appreciate the Cult for what they are. A great, sky-punching, anthemic, stadium rock band.

This album starts strongly with

Sun King

and continues in much the same vein. It perhaps becomes a bit samey after five tracks, but many bands are just as culpable of this.

The real star here is Billy Duffy. Just a great guitar performance all the way through. Really easy to enjoy this album.

Brad Summers

: Amazing album, one of my favourites of all time.

Edie (Ciao Baby)

is one of the greatest songs ever, but all songs have aged really well

John Davidson

: The first half of this album is wall-to-wall classic rock. They maintained their slightly gothic medicine man vibes but infused them with the spirit of Led Zeppelin too, deftly managing to land on the side of homage rather than ripoff.

I'm always wary of bands that don't have a stable lineup, but Astbury, Duffy and Stewart managed to create three classic rock albums in a row without holding on to a drummer so what do I know?

If the album stopped with

Soul Asylum

it would be short but perfect. As it stands, the remaining tracks bar

Soldier Blue

are all serviceable B-sides rather than essential.

Mike Canoe

: When Sonic Temple came out, I remember thinking that if a band's going to sell out, this was the way to do it. A big walloping arena-sized sound that brought together the best elements of the previous two albums, the psychedelic goth of

Love

and the frenzied AC/DC worship of

Electric

. (First studio album

Dreamtime

was in the import bin and out of my price range.)

Side one (as those of us born in the mid to late 1900s call it) was damn near perfect. It kicked off with the one-two punch of

Sun King

and

Fire Woman

and then picked things up by slowing them down with the absolutely massive-sounding

American Horse,

that also served as a callback for Billy Duffy and Ian Astbury's fascination with the American West.

Edie (Ciao Baby)

was a solid if dark-tinged ballad that had my friends and me trying to find out everything we could about Edie Sedgwick and Andy Warhol's Factory scene in the pre-internet dark ages.

And then there's

Sweet Soul Sister

, which is, to my mind, everything that's great about the Cult compressed into one song. Astbury takes his male gaze fetishism of women to a religious level, while the opening organs and closing choir sell the "sonic temple" concept better than anything on the album.

She Sells Sanctuary

as a

Love Removal Machine

.

Side two was a pretty big letdown, with raver

New York City

being the only song that merited repeated listens from me once I upgraded my cassette to CD. I may be one of the few Zeppelin fans on earth who thinks

Kashmir

is just OK, and so it goes with

Soul Asylum

, which was obviously inspired by it. The last three songs sounded like serviceable imitations of what came before.

"

This is where it all ends...

" The opening lines of the album seemed to be prophetic for the Cult. The band always had a drummer problem almost as bad as Spinal Tap's, but with the loss of bassist Jamie Stewart, the band became a "band" of Duffy and Astbury and whoever else. And while they may have released an occasional banger and could still put on a great show,

Sonic Temple

was the only time the Cult were a mainstream religion.

Final score: 8.45 (101 votes cast, total score 854)

pending_news.rss_body:
Greta Van Fleet

frontman Josh Kiszka has reflected on the dismay with which his band's early success was greeted by some members of the rock fraternity.

In an exclusive interview in the

current edition of

Classic Rock

magazine

, Kiszka recalls the reaction to GVF's breakthrough, when the band's soaring popularity was accompanied by a very vocal minority who hated what they were doing.

"When we came along, I think people were so concerned we were going to penetrate their hallowed rock'n'roll world, y'know, their religious temple, this bunch of snot-nosed kids wanting to change things up," he says. "But it was quite the antithesis. It was our respect for the genre. We just wanted to do something new, to move things along."

Kiszka goes on to reveal how some of the attacks affected him personally, so he did the most sensible thing.

“I stopped reading them," he says. "I’m fairly sensitive, so I thought, ‘This is weighing on my consciousness.’ I don’t even know the name of the publication, but someone said we were a bunch of talentless musicians who don’t know how to write a song or perform it. Things like that stab you where you’re tender. Some of that I carry. But I don’t believe it.

“I had a vocal coach come to our show in New York,” he continues. “It was our first outdoor amphitheatre/arena-type thing. She saw the show, then told me backstage she was one of those people who thought, ‘How dare they!’ But she said: ‘You deserve everything that is coming to you, and thank you for carrying the torch.’ So her tune changed very quickly."

pending_news.title: Q&A: Chuck Billy on His New memoir, ‘Holding My Breath: The Two Testaments of Chuck Billy’
pending_news.rss_body:
Metal fans may think they know Chuck Billy, the larger-than-life frontman of thrash metal titans

Testament

. But do they know the man behind the band?

Co-written with Dave Erickson, with a foreword by Judas Priest legend Rob Halford and an afterword from Lamb of God’s Randy Blythe, Billy is set to release his debut memoir,

Holding My Breath: The Two Testaments of Chuck Billy.

And while the unflinching look at the soon-to-be sixty-five-year-old frontman outlines his rise to become one of thrash metal’s most beloved figures, this is in no way a Testament book or standard rock ‘n’ roll tell-all.

Holding My Breath

is broken into what Billy calls his “Two Testaments,” the first following his upbringing in a resilient Native American and Mexican-American family and his introduction to the exploding Bay Area scene. The second walks with Billy through his battle with a rare form of cancer, germ cell seminoma, at 38 years old and the remarkable comeback story that followed.

Ahead of the book’s release, Billy sat down with

Decibel

for a candid Q&A, reflecting on his career, his decision to venture into the literary world, his spiritual awakening and thoughts on new material and the road ahead.

Chuck, how’s everything? How was your summer? I know you had a busy touring schedule there for a bit.

Chuck:

Summer was great. We’ve never gone back to Europe twice in a summer during festival season. We did this year, and it went really well. It was a long trip, but I like how we broke it up. Great shows. We got to hook up with our friends on the off shows with Armored Saint, Metal Church and Death Angel. So it was cool that we got to spend some time with some friends. It’s been good. We’ve been home. Eric and Chris have been diving into new music. They’ve got enough to start going and make another record. Hopefully, we plan to get in the studio next July. So we’ve got another record ready to go already.

In terms of the new music, I’ve heard you say loads of times you always want to keep pushing yourselves, try new things, experiment. Particularly in this early stage now, well before you get in the studio, how do you see the germ of, okay, here’s what we want a new Testament record to be?

Chuck:

Well, we don’t ever do that. We don’t say this is what we want it to be because it’s never the same. Our records never are coming off the last one ever. So it’s about whatever feels good. And again, and I think I share in the book towards the end how, you know, in the early years, me holding my breath, as you will, being a little stubborn in the songwriting and what I sing over, it maybe threw a wrench in the process. The songs came out great, but maybe I just stalled it up a little bit, just going against the grain for a minute, thinking I know, but I don’t know. But I think when I started loosening up, like on the

Titans

record, and especially this last record, just taking the music, listening to the shit out of it, and coming up with the best I can without changing anything. And it ended up making it more challenging for me vocally. Made me in an uncomfortable place, which I thought made for more creativity, but also made me a little nervous and scared too because Eric and Chris are writing some really aggressive modern Testament than we have. So again, it’s another thing for me to go, okay, holy shit, I gotta kind of keep up. So I find now that it’s definitely where we’re at; it’s definitely a different band, for sure.

Yeah, and you mentioned trying to fit into the mould of what these guys are bringing you. “For the Love of Pain” in particular on the new record is a song that just whops you over the fucking head. And you have to meet that too, because the guys are coming at 5,000 miles an hour, and you’re needing to bring it. It’s modern, it’s really heavy, but it’s not a throwback song to what someone might expect when they hear Testament. How does a track like that, where you really challenge yourself, present live?

Chuck:

Well, I was just about to say, in the live situation, we’ve opened with it. We put it right up at the top of the set in the first couple of songs, because it hits pretty good. And I think on the last tour, we really wanted to introduce three of the new songs. We played three new ones back to back, like I think it was three, four, and five or something in the show. So we jumped right in, right away, a couple of old-school, and then hit them hard with three new ones.

Yeah, that’s the cool thing at this point, too, where you can kind of tailor the set list, and you have enough of a discography now that you can play the hits, play some oddities, some B-sides, and then we can hit them with some new stuff. It’s a nice place to be.

Chuck:

And it’s good for us because you put out records; you can’t sing and play all your records ever for any band. So I think the times of making records, you aren’t looking to get an hour of music. We’ve got to have 10 songs. I think that tension span isn’t that long. And you could probably still get away with 45 minutes and eight songs or so, eight solid five-minute killers. Times are changing. I think that’s why now we’re like, we don’t need to go write 15 songs and put together a record. Let’s focus on getting 10, and maybe we’ll have eight on the record. You know, it depends on how long they are, but I think right now we’re at about song 13, maybe 14 songs that we’ve got.

Before we get into the book, I know you’re going back to Europe next year to support Megadeth. Obviously, they’re guys you know quite well who are kind of wrapping things up to a degree. Just your thoughts on Megadeth, what they’ve meant to thrash, and what they meant to you as friends and tourmates.

Chuck:

Well, we got a lot of history. We supported each other in the early years. Dave emceed a lot of our shows in LA in the 87/88 years, somewhere around there. They took us on tour. Over the years, we became good friends and worked closely with management companies together. Just a lot. I mean, we have a lot of history, and we have some ups and downs, but I don’t think it’s bad enough ups and downs to stop us from touring together and working together, you know? But I think Megadeth, what they added and what Dave brought to it, is very important because he was a key part of that early Metallica stuff. And for him to lose that and go off in his own and really make a claim to who he is as a songwriter and riff writer and hooks and all that, he’s right there in the class of Metallica. So for him to prosper and make his own name for himself and career, fuck yeah, hell yeah. I think that’s great. And for what they do as far as style of metal, they’ve written some great stuff and are still writing great stuff. So again, Dave, he’s a staple of what we’re doing here, and for him to maybe draw a line in the sand and say, okay, this is going to be it sometime. Yeah, that’s it. Pretty cool, big of them. And I don’t know what the underscore of that is and the reasoning, but I think we’ve all got to find that comes eventually.

Moving to the book. You’ve mentioned it before that you’re a pretty private guy when it comes down to it. Was this a bit of a reach for you to think, “Are people gonna wanna hear what I have to say” type thing? Because you’re a humble guy, you’re a private guy from everything I know of you. Was it a lot to take on to be like, okay, where do I start? Take me through that.

Chuck:

Pretty much. I mean, when I was first approached a while back, I put it on the back burner because I was kind of like busy; I don’t know if I have a year to commit, and it sounds like a pain in the ass, all the above. And it was brought to me, and so I kind of just put it on the back burner, and as time went by, it got brought up, and the timing just happened to be that, okay, the record came out last year, we’re touring on it. You know, I’ve got a break now, and we’re writing, but still have a break. If I’m going to commit now is the only window I really have right after the record comes out, and we’re done with a little bit of touring. So I committed. Next thing you know, I had a literary agent, and I was off and running. I mean, it happens so fast in this business compared to the business where you take your time till it’s ready and write. This was like, ready, set, go. And everything was just like, okay, we need this, we need that. And I mean, fast. I was like, wow, I haven’t even had time to think. And so when we first did it, it was like, okay, you guys got to write a manuscript; I’ll shop it around, then we’ll start writing once we get the deal; you’ll probably take a year for this. And the next thing, a week later, it’s like shit; I got offers already. You know, let’s look at these. I picked one and said, okay, let’s go with this company. It’s going to be a good company. Here are some writers; meet these guys, pick David. And then it was just like, okay, here we go. First phone call, “Hey David, how you doing?” You know, and that was kind of odd. Like, okay, “Well, I’ve never done this. You’ve got a couple of bestsellers. Where do we want to start? How do we wanna start? I don’t know, have a title for this, or I don’t know what I want, but what I do want to get across, first of all, this is not a Testament book. I want to make sure that, you know, it’s not a testament book.” What I enjoy when I read autobiographies or other memoirs from people, I like to know who they are before the celebrity, or who they are before what we all know them as. And I enjoy that part of books when I read that. So I wanted to convey that. And I thought, maybe because of the part of holding my breath and my story, everything that happened, looking back and talking through it, that’s when it kind of all came together as the title, holding my breath. Let’s start back at eight months old. Wow. And then to talk through your life and to see how that holding-your-breath phrase and being stubborn, getting your way and what that meant throughout life. And as I did the book, kind of looking at it and reflecting and thinking, well, maybe that stubborn kid holding his breath was getting ready to hold his breath when he had to fight cancer because I was supposed to die at 38. And maybe something in the universe shifted, and I got through it, whatever way I did, but I found my way through it. And on the other side was this whole new life and Chuck and view of the world and the band. And so we kind of found our story and how we were going to work it and put it together and come up with the title as we worked. So it was a really weird thing. It’s definitely therapeutic. I was getting to enjoy it after a while. It really wasn’t a pain in the ass, and we really knocked it out. I got with him three or four days a week, so we weren’t farting around. I guess maybe they thought a year was cause we didn’t have time, but we talked a lot and got it done.

And you really hit on it there, getting in sync with your writing partner, like that’s no easy thing at all, finding the rhythm and direction. And then you have that dividing line of, we know where we’re going with the two testaments, before and after the illness to a degree. How did you land on the two-testament idea?

Chuck:

I came up with the picture idea of half a live shot, half the native shot because I knew the native healing was a part of the story. So when I saw the picture and showed it to the writer, he kind of came up with, “Whoa, the Two Testaments of Chuck.” There are two Chucks. And then we’re like, whoa. Okay, the Two Testaments. We like that because it’s nice to fit the name Testament in the title somewhere in there. Okay, well, then that makes sense. Let’s go with that. I like that. And it’s two stories. So now we’ve got our outline. The two Chucks before and after, the two testaments before and after, and then really dive into the crossroads in the middle of the cancer and the benefit show and all that stuff and what happened because of that and surviving, not going at 38. Again, the universe had a different plan because if Pamela Spivey never knocked on my door that day and brought a buyer to my house, I would have never sold my house. I never would have gone and seen the doctor. My tumour probably would have erupted. And I would have died at 38, just like the plan was supposed to happen, but something else in the universe happened. And I guess that’s when I really kind of looked back; now it’s been 25 years. Man, I made some good records. I’ve been very lucky with the band, and where we’re at today, shit, you know, maybe it is time to tell the story and document it.

Yeah, and from what I’ve seen since then, you’ve become a very spiritual person, and not so much a “religious” person, but spirituality. Talk me through that and how the last 25 years have been in terms of your journey and discovering who you are.

Chuck:

Well, yeah, I mean, I was raised a Catholic. My mom’s very religious. So I was raised with all those stories and beliefs, but then getting the opportunity to travel the world, meet a bunch of different people and cultures and understand other beliefs and other powers out there. It opened my eyes to, like, wow, maybe there’s not just one God. Maybe there are multiple gods or multiple beliefs or multiple higher powers, whatever you want to call it, in different religions in different parts of the world. And I was even open to the aliens creating mankind, writing records about that, you know? So I’m way out there. It’s just a trip, the way it all worked out religiously. Cause after I did the native healing and went through some very unbelievable that after telling, you almost people aren’t gonna believe this, but it was what happened, it made me think that I’m more spiritual. I want to call myself spiritual, not a religious person. Yeah, I was raised Catholic, but if someone goes, “What are you?” I’d say I’m spiritual; I’m not gonna go “I’m a catholic.”

Is there anything from this so far that people, whoever’s had a chance to see it, are surprised to read or learn about you? Whether it’s post-cancer or young Chuck? Is there something you think fans, readers, will be surprised by in particular?

Chuck:

Well, no, but I just think the story of the kid holding his breath, how he was raised. And I mean, I think the other big flip side of this whole story too is my parents. My four brothers and I are like miracle children. Two of them survived tuberculosis and then started a family late in life. First of all, that right there, and then for them to have another chance at life and have a family. Man, they’d do anything for us kids, you know? So that’s why I think my father protected us, raised us, taught us, and so maybe all those lessons going through that were preparing me for that battle.

It’s wild to think back on some of the coincidences and some of, if you didn’t go this way, what would have happened this way? It kind of blows your mind sometimes.

Chuck:

And that’s the interesting thing about doing a book or doing the memoir is it’s never easy talking about yourself for three or four months. That’s never easy, and I had to bring in my wife, bandmates, friends, old band members to talk with my writer and me because we would share stories and all of a sudden be like, “Oh, did you tell them this story?” Oh yeah, I forgot about that, and next we’re off in a story, so it helped that, and there are so many more stories. That book could have been a thousand pages if we really wanted to keep going crazy, but I really just wanted to convey that young kid holding his breath and who he is. That no matter what, at the end of the day, 10 years, 20 years down the road, someone reads this book that knew who that kid was, that was the lead singer of Testament. You know, it’s all right there.

Absolutely. I don’t think I’ve ever asked you this, but were there some definitive artists, musicians, albums that really broke you into rock music and heavy music? Everyone has those gateway bands, right? I know for me, in the beginning it was KISS, and that opened the floodgates. What was it for you?

Chuck:

Well, it was definitely KISS, but KISS was more of an introduction to big shows, big theatrics, but I loved the music, so seeing it was awesome. But I think for a darker side and heavier side, I started paying attention to more guitar; it would have to be Black Sabbath. I mean, that Black Sabbath,

We Sold Our Soul for Rock ‘n’ Roll

. The album vinyl cover, to me, was the scariest, heaviest thing lying in your room, just staring at that open gatefold, hearing the rain and the bells tolling and the album starting, like, wow, holy shit, what is this? I mean, those were, like, to me, this is scary. And I guess that’s what they were shooting for.

It’s funny now because you hear Sabbath on classic rock radio or rock radio, or whatever. I can’t imagine what it must have been like at the time. People hearing and seeing Sabbath for the first time. It must have just shattered people’s minds.

Chuck:

It blew minds. I mean, just how dark it was. Just a fucking black album with the title. That’s it. You open it up, the lady lying in a coffin, you know, like holy shit. Okay. This is going to be good.

Moving forward, obviously you mentioned this was a very cathartic process for you. We talked about Megadeth kind of winding things down. It feels like you guys are still firing on a cylinder, still excited about where you’re heading towards another record. What keeps you motivated? What keeps you going? And how do you see the next 10 years going in a perfect world?

Chuck:

Well, I think at this point, what keeps us motivated is that we’re 40 years into it. I know we’ve got a couple of records left under Nuclear Blast, so we know that’s going to take some time. I don’t know, really, cause we’ll be ready to do another record, and I’m sure we’ll have enough for the next. So we’ll deliver those two records pretty quickly. We’ll see what happens if we sign some more records with them. Who knows. But again, I think we’re all in a really good spot health-wise, headspace-wise. There’s no reason yet to think about that day. We have talked to our agents and said, let’s just put a time window, the best of or worst-case scenarios. Let’s talk about the next six, seven years. And we’ve done that this summer with our agents in Europe and in America just said, let’s see what that looks like. And if we do deliver records, what’s that gonna look like for us? And how old are we gonna be then? You know what I mean? It’s six years. I’m gonna be 70 years old. That’s gonna go by pretty quick. You know, at 70, shit, how’s my body gonna be reacting at that age? Right now, today, I could say I feel great. Six years from now? Now I feel awesome, but we’ll see what happens in that time window. So in a perfect world, I could drag it out for 20 years, but we don’t have that. So that’s why I think we’re motivated, and let’s just keep making music. We’re inspired. We’re putting out some good tunes and records. We got people still coming to the shows, buying records. The label wants us. Let’s just keep going till we can’t, I guess.

Psychedelic Oklahomans

The Flaming Lips

have announced

The Teardrop Throbs

, their 17th studio album and their first since 2020's

American Head

. The album will be released via Third Man Records on January 22, and is the band's first since the departure of longtime members Michael Ivins in 2021 and Steven Drozd three years later.

The Teardrop Throbs

was produced by the band with Taylor Johnson, Dave Fridmann and Scott Booker, with additional production from Jon Fridmann and Mike Fridmann. The band have also released the first single from the new album, the typically transcendent

God Will Control The Werewolves.

"

Control The Werewolves

started as a little story about my two boys (Bloom and Rex) and me playing hide and seek at the park as it was getting dark outside," says Lips frontman Kevin Coyne. "We had all become very aware of the moon cycles when we stayed at an ocean view Airbnb about a month previously.

"The full moon had sucked all the water out of this ocean cove area, and we walked a quarter mile out on the seabed, seeing strange ocean creatures attached to the rocks. But yes... because of the moon, we had this amazing adventure, so it was fresh in our minds, and on this evening of hide-and-seek, it was luckily another full moon.

"Bloom asked me if, while he and Rex were hiding, the werewolves would get them (they had also watched a few werewolf movies and knew that the full moon was the time when the werewolves were out and about), and I told him God would control the werewolves for a little bit while we played hide-and-seek.

"The way I heard the song sounding (in my head) was kind of

Pink Floyd

's

The Dark Side Of The Moon,

but Syd Barrett is still in the band. Ha!"

The Teardrop Throbs

Iron Maiden

singer

Bruce Dickinson

has announced a string of European and UK tour dates for summer, autumn and winter 2026.

The mercurial frontman will hit the road with his solo band on the

Psychogod

tour from June to July, where he’ll play headline dates and a number of festival sets. He’ll return to the road from November to December for a headline run where he’ll be supported by Swedish prog/power metal band Evergrey.

Tickets go on sale on Friday, October 30. See dates below.

Dickinson comments: “What we do is real and that’s so important right now. A real drummer, a real bass player, real guitarists, real keyboards – A.I. can only copy, it can only pretend. It can never be in love, and it can never play. This band? They can really play!”

The singer’s live lineup will be rounded out by guitarists Chris Declercq and Philip Näslund, bassist Tanya O’Callaghan, keyboardist Mistheria and drummer Dave Moreno. The tour comes after the group spent much of 2026 recording Dickinson’s upcoming solo album, the follow-up to 2024’s

The Mandrake Project

. Press materials say that the newly announced shows will “showcase a whole range of new material, alongside fan favourites and deep cuts spanning his entire solo career”.

Dickinson told VSX over the summer that

his new album will be out next year and is “heavy as shit”

. It was recorded live in the studio in early 2026, with tracking taking place at Studio 606 in Los Angeles, the space owned by Foo Fighters frontman Dave Grohl. Members of Brazilian heavy metal greats Sepultura are set to appear.

As well as touring with his solo band, Dickinson will hit the road with Iron Maiden next year, despite the band previously stating their ongoing 2026 dates will be their last until at least 2028. The British institution

will play a string of North American dates in the spring

pending_news.title: Listen: Venomous Echoes Explore the Dark Side of Death Metal on Violator of Mater
pending_news.rss_body:
Successfully making four records in as many years is an impressive feat no matter how you slice it but Ohio black/death metal outfit

Venomous Echoes

, the product of one Ben Vanweelden, take it a step beyond. Initially forming in 2020, Venomous Echoes began releasing full-length albums in 2023, with the most recent being

Ŋvęŧş-Violator of Mater

, released earlier this year by I, Voidhanger.

Arriving in September,

Ŋvęŧş-Violator of Mater

builds on the framework laid on previous albums but pushes it further. Opener “Dysmor Opens” sets the tone with spacey synthesizers, which can be heard layered throughout the album. From there, Venomous Echoes are off to the races, ripping through a collection of songs that plumb the darker, more twisted side of death metal. Produced by Stephen Knapp, who also programmed drums throughout the album,

Ŋvęŧş-Violator of Mater

is twisting and, at times, overwhelming. The guitars and spastic drum programming create a thick vortex, with the only light coming from the previously mentioned synth parts, as heard on “Æhɔɲ” and “Çịrẹ.” Even the acoustic respite on “Monolith of Purity” is distorted and modified, like a dread-inducing rug pull.

Like previous albums, Vanweelden uses Venomous Echoes as an outlet to explore real-life trauma and mental health issues. Even if the words he screams, howls and growls aren’t intelligible, the pain and anger in those words is palpable.

Violator of Mater

is out now on I, Voidhanger. If you’re willing to dive into the darkness, it’s one of the year’s most interesting death metal releases.

pending_news.title: Get in the Halloween spirit by having Kirk Hammett read you Edgar Allen Poe, soundtracked by a Metallica song
pending_news.rss_body:
Metallica

’s Kirk Hammett has helped usher in Halloween by reading

The Raven

by Edgar Allen Poe.

On Tuesday (October 27), San Francisco’s thrash metal giants got their lead guitarist and resident horror hound to chill fans with the 1845 poem, long a staple of Gothic literature, soundtracked by the song

Inamorata

from their 2023 album

72 Seasons

. Watch below.

Hammett has made no secret of his lifelong love for horror. He has an array of ESP KH-2 guitars decorated to feature iconic scary film figures, with respective models depicting Boris Karloff as Frankenstein’s monster, Bela Lugosi as Count Dracula and Elsa Lanchester as The Bride in

Bride Of Frankenstein

.

Another model is designed to resemble a Ouija board: a fixture of horror films since one was used to inadvertently summon the demon Pazuzu in the 1973 classic

The Exorcist

.

In addition, Hammett, 63, hosted the horror convention Kirk Von Hammett’s Fear FestEvil from 2014 to 2015. The events featured live performances, signings and panels all rooted in the guitarist’s passion for the spooky.

During a 2022 interview with Gibson Guitars, Hammett spoke about how 1974’s

The Texas Chain Saw Massacre

“truly” frightened him growing up.

“There was a buzz on the street and everyone was talking about it,” he said. “I remember going to see it and truly being frightened because there hadn’t been a film like that up to that point that was so graphic and violent in its brutality. There wasn’t anything like that. I remember me and my friends leaving the theatre shaking our heads going, ‘Wow’, and looking at each other wondering, ‘Did we just see that?!’ It was a real experience.”

He also spoke about

The Exorcist

, explaining how it affected him as a Catholic kid: “I thought the perpetrators of that film were coming after me next,” he said. “It was an honest fear when we were kids. For the next four months I slept with the lights on every single night.”

Hammett joined Metallica in 1983, shortly before the recording of their 1983 debut album

Kill ’Em All

, and has been with the band ever since. One of the biggest acts in heavy metal, they’ve sold more than 150 million albums worldwide and won 10 Grammy Awards.

The four-piece are currently putting on a residency at Las Vegas multimedia venue the Sphere, scheduled to continue on Thursday (October 29), then on Halloween night itself on Saturday. Whether Hammett will dress up to mark the occasion remains to be seen.

Minneapolis duo

Cavernous Maw

expand their vision with the release of its brand-new single and video,

“The Yeti Approaches the Wall,”

the first offering from the forthcoming album

Ancestral Lands Beyond the Antarctic Ice Wall

,

slated for release at a later date.

​

Blending relentless death metal intensity with emotional weight, memorable melodies, and unexpected influences drawn from black metal,

technical death metal

, and classic extreme metal,

“The Yeti Approaches the Wall”

marks the next evolutionary step for the two-piece act.

Comprised of longtime friends and collaborators Niilo Smith (vocals/guitar) and Ben Fagerness (drums),

Cavernous Maw

were born from a desire to strip away complications and focus purely on creating music. After years of playing together in various projects, the pair embraced the simplicity and creative freedom of a two-member lineup, forging a sound that is equal parts brutal, dynamic, and unmistakably their own.

​

The new single showcases a more mature and refined version of the vision first introduced on their debut EP,

Primitive.

​

​

​

“;The Yeti Approaches the Wall’ was the first song we wrote for our first full-length. It started as nearly all of our songs do: the two of us jamming in the practice space, locking onto a riff and expanding it. The arrangement and drum parts were carefully crafted to keep the energy flowing from beginning to end. Lyrically, the song is about exactly what the title suggests: a yeti approaching a wall. Whether that wall is physical or mental is up to the listener,” says

Fagerness.

​

Serving as the opening chapter of a larger concept, the track introduces listeners to a mysterious protagonist embarking on a journey beyond the boundaries of his known world. Throughout

Ancestral Lands Beyond the Antarctic Ice Wall,

the album follows the yeti’s path of discovery, curiosity, growth, understanding, and ultimately, humanity’s downfall.

Korn

have returned to the British Isles for the first time since headlining Download festival in June 2025.

The Bakersfield nu metal pioneers put on their first of six shows in England and the Republic Of Ireland on Monday (October 26), where they played an 18-song set including such 90s hits as

Blind

,

Freak On A Leash

and

Falling Away From Me

at First Direct Bank Arena in Leeds.

They also dusted off 1996 rarity

Chi

, which before this tour hadn’t played since 2013, and

Kill You

, unplayed since 2007. See the full setlist and watch videos below.

Korn are still touring to promote their 2022 album

Requiem

, though they haven’t played any songs from the record on this run. However, they have been performing

Reward The Scars

, the single they put out in April

in collaboration with role-playing videogame

Diablo IV

.

Whether the song will make the tracklisting of the band’s next record, their 15th overall, remains to be seen. Last month, Ray Luzier’s technician revealed that the drummer

has recorded his parts for the release

.

Korn’s 15th album will be their first without co-founding bassist Reginald “Fieldy” Arvizu, who parted ways with the band shortly after completing his work on

Requiem

. Roberto “Ra” Díaz has been filling in live since late 2021. This year, Fieldy explained why and his former bandmates parted ways, revealing that it came down to his refusal to get the COVID-19 vaccine, and his resultant inability to tour internationally.

“COVID happened,” he told the

Shady Characters

podcast. “That’s it. I’m like, ‘I’m not going out there.’ That’s what happened, ’cause it was new. Now. I didn’t get vaccinated or anything – but when you reflect on it, that’s what happened. They’re like, ‘We’re going to Florida,’ and I’m like, ‘I’m not going to get vaccinated. I’m not going.’ I go, ‘People, this is weird right now.’”

Korn’s UK/Ireland tour continues on Thursday (October 28) at Utilita Arena in Birmingham, then will proceed through Manchester and Dublin before concluding at London’s O2 Arena on November 4. They’ll return to mainland Europe on November 8, when they play the Ziggo Dome in Amsterdam. The tour will wrap up at Unipol Forum in Assago, Italy on November 21.

pending_news.title: Live Review: DYING FETUS and SANGUISUGABOGG at Emo’s (Austin, TX – 10/15/26)
pending_news.rss_body:
review by Gerard Cosloy

photos by Angela Betancourt

For starters, I would like sincerely apologize to

Deterioration, Left To Suffer

and the venerable

Crowbar

for missing their sets ; I’d been on the phone all evening with Kalshi customer support—it seems someone ran up several thousand dollars of charges to my credit card making trades last weekend on whether or not James Hetfield would use his Sphere platform to make a political statement. The bad news is, my dog’s college fund was cleaned out. On the bright side, I had exactly enough cash left over for

Sanguisugabogg

’s BLUEY ON A STABBING SPREE shirt, so it’s not a total disaster.

Emo’s, for those who’ve not been, is a charmless, character-free aircraft hanger on our city’s southeastern side and aside from the brand name, cannot be confused with the deeply beloved punk dump that operated downtown for ages. Were Columbus’ Sanguisugabogg capable of teleporting themselves back to those halcyon days, they’d undoubtedly be right at home in said squalid, chaotic environment. Semi-plagued with a FOH mix I will charitably describe as boomy-as-fook, the band managed, regardless to trundle their way thru a smattering of career highlights showcasing their considerable range (songs about tearing someone’s face off, killing people, killing people and turning them into furniture, etc.)  While this was my first time seeing them since the recent exit of Cedrik Davis and Cody Davidson’s transition from drums to guitar, this was not appreciably different than their last headline appearance in Austin some 11 months ago (OK, there was at least one more fight and I would like that officially noted at setlist.fm).  There’s no denying they bring the brutality with wit and panache, I just wish it was twice as loud (and perhaps it is just that on other occasions—also, I cannot hear for shit)

Superficial similarities aside,

Dying Fetus’

presentation was a study in contrasts and deft execution—the level of technical proficiency is off the charts (assuming there’s a chart for such things) and IN SPITE OF THIS they’re as deliberately bludgeoning as any rival you care to cite. Guitarist/vocalist John Gallagher—the lone remaining founding member—is all business (singing about unmitigated carnage is his business and business is growing at steady clip, as the saying goes). The cliché “foundational band” gets tossed around for ensembles working atop paper mache far too often but in this case, it couldn’t be more true. We’re beyond lucky to be living and breathing in a world where Dying Fetus cast such an immense creative shadow, which is slightly ironic given the subject matter extols the virtues of well, stuff that’s the opposite of living and breathing.

Angela Betancourt
